title: Uni- versus bilateral cerebral perfusion in hemiarch replacement – a prospective randomized controlled trial
summary:
What Is This Study About?
This study looks at how best to protect the brain during a specific type of heart surgery known as "aortic hemiarch replacement," which is performed when part of the main blood vessel leading from the heart (the aorta) needs to be repaired or replaced due to disease.

Why Is This Study Being Done?
During this surgery, doctors must temporarily stop blood flow in the aorta. Because the brain still needs oxygen during this time, doctors use special techniques to keep the brain supplied with blood. There are two main ways to do this:

Unilateral (one-sided) brain blood flow: Blood is sent through just one artery to supply the brain.

Bilateral (two-sided) brain blood flow: Blood is supplied to both sides of the brain through two arteries.

Both methods are used in hospitals, but it is unclear which is better at preventing complications like stroke or other brain injuries. This study aims to find out if the simpler one-sided approach is just as safe and effective as the two-sided method.

What Will Happen in the Study?
Patients needing non-emergent aortic hemiarch surgery will be invited to join. With their permission, they are randomly assigned to receive either the one-sided or two-sided brain protection technique during their operation. Doctors and nurses will carefully monitor each patient during and after surgery. No extra blood draws or special tests are needed for the study beyond normal hospital care.

What Does the Study Hope to Learn?
The main focus is to see how many eligible patients can be recruited and how well the process works for a future larger study. The researchers will also look to see:

How often patients have a stroke or other brain complications
How often other problems like kidney issues, confusion, or lung complications occur after surgery
Whether switching from one method to the other is needed during surgery

Why Is This Important?
This research may help doctors choose the safest and most effective brain protection method for this type of heart surgery in the future. The results could help set new standards so that every patient gets the best possible care.

interventions.name: Patients undergoing non-emergent aortic hemiarch replacement with unilateral antegrade cerebral perfusion. This does not significantly prolong or alter the operation performed. Only the type of cerebral perfusion changes. Patients also do not undergo any altered post- or preoperative diagnostics.

Patients undergoing non-emergent aortic hemiarch replacement with bilateral antegrade cerebral perfusion. This does not significantly prolong or alter the operation performed. Only the type of cerebral perfusion changes. Patients also do not undergo any altered post- or preoperative diagnostics.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with ascending aortic and proximal aortic arch aneurysm with indication for non-emergent surgical replacement according to the 2023 EACTS/STS Guidelines for diagnosing and treating acute and chronic syndromes of the aortic organ.
Exclusion criteria:
Patients younger than 18 years 
Severe calcification of the aortic arch or supra aortic vessels 
Pregnant and breastfeeding women 
Patients unable to give informed consent (psychiatric disease, forms of dementia, substance abuse, etc.) 
Acute neurological deficit (< 3 months) 
Patients without informed consent
